Mom's Deed, Policies and Account Papers in One Place

An organizer for families planning ahead: where each paper is, how recent it is, who holds it, and which ones haven't turned up.

Download PDF

The deed is in Mom's safe-deposit box, the life insurance policy is in a folder somewhere, and nobody remembers whether there's a trust.

This page doesn't ask you to read or understand any of it. Go through it with Mom when it suits her, and for each paper write where it is, the date on it, and who holds it.

What to collectWhere it isIts dateWho has it
Deed to her home
Latest property tax bill, and papers for any mortgage or loan on the home
Social Security and pension paperwork
Recent statements for checking, savings and investment accounts
Recent statements for retirement accounts
Life insurance policies
Annuity contracts
Papers for anything owned jointly with someone else
Trust documents, if there is a trust
Records of significant gifts, transfers or ownership changes in recent years
If Mom is married: the same papers for her spouse

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What hasn't turned up yet, and who will look for it

Anything above with an empty line. Put a name next to each.

For example Nobody has seen the deed. Mom thinks it's in the safe-deposit box; she and Denise will look the next time they're at the bank.

Today's date, and when you'll go through this again

The page describes one day. Say which day, and pick a time to look at it again that suits Mom.

For example Filled in with Mom on a Sunday in October. We'll go through it again next fall, or sooner if something changes.

How to use it

  • Write the date printed on each paper. If it has no date, write “undated.”
  • Leave account numbers, Social Security numbers and passwords off this page. Just say where the paper is.
  • Don't rewrite or summarize a document here, and don't move one without Mom knowing where it went.
  • If nobody knows whether something exists, a trust for instance, write “don't know.” That's a finished line.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any deed, policy, statement or trust means, and it doesn't say how any of them would be looked at if Mom ever applied for Medicaid. Rules vary by state, so those questions go to your Medicaid planner or the appropriate licensed professional. Nothing here is legal, financial or tax advice.
